title: Invitations, feasts and visiting etiquette
goal: Inviting, accepting invitations and behaving properly in a Malaysian home — and mastering the word *jemput*, which works quite differently from what you might expect.
bekal: inviting, and accepting or declining invitations politely

dialogs.title: Dialogue — A wedding invitation
dialogs.intro: In the cafeteria, Haziq hands Sarah a gold-colored card.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Sarah, ni kad jemputan. Kakak saya nak kahwin bulan depan.
lines.id: Sarah, here's an invitation card. My sister is getting married next month.
lines.literal: Sarah, this card invitation. older-sister my want marry month front.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Dua belas haribulan, hari Ahad. Kat kampung, Kuala Selangor.
lines.id: The twelfth, a Sunday. In our home village, Kuala Selangor.
lines.literal: two ten day-month, day Sunday. at village, Kuala Selangor.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Jauh tak? Saya kena naik apa?
lines.id: Is it far? How do I get there?
lines.literal: far not? I must ride what?

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Sejam setengah je. Ikut kereta saya, boleh tumpang.
lines.id: Only an hour and a half. Come in my car, you can get a ride.
lines.literal: one-hour half just. follow car my, can ride-along.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Alhamdulillah. Saya kena bawa apa-apa tak?

lines.literal: praise-God. I must bring anything not?

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Tak payah. Kalau nak, bawa duit dalam sampul je. Tapi tak wajib.
lines.id: No need. If you want, just bring some money in an envelope. But it's not compulsory.

lines.text: Pakaian macam mana? Saya tak ada baju kurung.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Sopan je dah cukup. Tapi kalau nak beli baju kurung pun boleh — kakak saya mesti suka.
lines.id: Something modest is enough. But you could buy a baju kurung too — my sister would love that.
lines.literal: modest just already enough. but if want buy baju kurung also can — older-sister my surely like.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Okey, saya cuba cari. Pukul berapa kena sampai?
lines.id: Okay, I'll try to find one. What time should I arrive?

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Kenduri mula pukul sebelas pagi sampai petang. Datang bila-bila pun boleh.

lines.text: Bagus. Jemput datang ya. Mak saya dah tanya pasal awak.
lines.id: Great. Do come, okay? My mum has already been asking about you.

notes: ⚠️ **Jemput** in Malay means **to invite** as well as to pick someone up. *Kad jemputan* = invitation card, *jemput datang* = please come, *saya dijemput ke kenduri* = I've been invited to a feast. The "pick up" meaning exists too (*jemput saya kat stesen* = pick me up at the station), so context decides.

**Tumpang** = to get a ride, to stay at someone's place, to share someone's space. *Boleh tumpang?* = "Can I get a ride?" It has a big family: *tumpang tanya* (excuse me, may I ask — unit 7), *penumpang* (passenger), *tumpang lalu* (excuse me, coming through).

**Kenduri** = a feast, celebration with a meal. *Kenduri kahwin* = wedding reception, *kenduri arwah* = prayer gathering for the deceased. In Malaysia it's the standard word for any celebration that involves eating together.
**Kahwin** = to marry. Spelled with *hw*; the more refined forms are *berkahwin* or *bernikah*. *Kahwin* is completely neutral and used on official documents (*taraf perkahwinan* = marital status).
**Sampul** = envelope. *Duit dalam sampul* = money in an envelope — the custom of giving a contribution at Malaysian feasts, and not at all expected of foreign guests.

grammars.title: Inviting, accepting and declining
body: Malay keeps three words apart: **jemput** (invite), **sila** (please, go ahead) and **tolong** (please help). Picking the wrong one sounds odd, though it rarely offends.

head: Use
Malay
English
rows: We invite you, sir, to attend.
Please come in. Please sit down.
If I'm blessed with the chance, I'll come.

after: ⚠️ **Jemput makan** is something you'll hear every time food is put on the table — it means "please eat", not "pick me up to eat". You're expected to respond by starting to eat, not by politely refusing three times.

**InsyaAllah** (God willing) needs careful reading. It can mean a sincere yes, or a very gentle no. The clue is in what comes next: if the person asks about the time and directions, they're really coming; if they change the subject right away, it's a no.

sections.title: Malaysian celebrations and what you need to know

head: Celebration
What it is
What to say
rows: Selamat Hari Raya, maaf zahir dan batin
Gong Xi Fa Cai / Selamat Tahun Baru Cina

blocks.text: **Rumah terbuka** (open house) is a Malaysian custom worth understanding: on any festival, families open their homes to anyone who comes — neighbors, colleagues, acquaintances, even strangers. No invitation card needed, no need to bring anything, and people of different religions visit each other's open houses. It's one of the best things about Malaysia, and as a newcomer you'll almost certainly be invited.

**Duit raya** is money in a green envelope that adults give to children and unmarried people at Hari Raya — similar to Chinese red packets (*angpau*). The amounts are small; what matters isn't the value. If you're young and unmarried you might receive one: accept it with both hands and say thank you.

blocks.title: Feast vocabulary
items: **pengantin** — bride or groom. **Raja sehari** — "king for a day", a name for the bridal couple.
**kompang** — large frame drums that accompany the bridal procession.
**bersanding** — the couple sitting side by side on the dais.
**hantaran** — wedding gift trays exchanged between families.
**kenduri arwah** — prayer gathering for the deceased.
**berbuka puasa** — breaking the fast. **Bazar Ramadan** — Ramadan food market.
**beraya / balik kampung** — celebrate Hari Raya / go back to your home village ⚠️

blocks.text: **Balik kampung** = going back to your home village. Before Hari Raya, Malaysia sees a huge exodus from the cities, and the whole thing is simply called *balik kampung*.
Much of this etiquette is common across Southeast Asia. Here's what to watch for:

items: **Greet at the door and wait for an answer.** *Assalamualaikum* to Muslim families; *Helo, ada orang?* (Hello, anyone home?) elsewhere. Don't go in until someone answers.
**Take your shoes off.** Almost every home in Malaysia expects it. Leave them neatly, facing outward.
**Accept food and drink with your right hand.** This matters and people notice.
**Don't refuse a drink.** If you really don't want it, accept it and take a sip. Refusing outright feels like rejecting your host's hospitality.
**Praise the food.** *Sedap sangat, mak cik!* (Delicious, auntie!) It's expected, not just politeness.
**Greet older people with a salam.** In Malay families, younger people take an elder's hand in both of theirs, bowing slightly, and may touch it to their forehead.
**Don't sit higher than older people** when everyone is on the floor, and don't step over anyone who is sitting.
**Say goodbye before leaving** and thank your host in person. *Terima kasih, mak cik. Saya balik dulu ya.* (Thank you, auntie. I'll be going now.)

blocks.title: Phrases for visiting
items: **Assalamualaikum. / Helo, ada orang?** — Hello, anyone home?
**Terima kasih jemput saya.** — Thanks for inviting me.
**Rumah mak cik cantik.** — You have a lovely home, auntie.
**Sedap sangat masakan ni.** — This food is delicious.
**Boleh tumpang tandas?** — May I use your bathroom?
**Saya balik dulu ya. Dah lambat.** — I'll be going now. It's getting late.
**Lain kali datang rumah saya pula.** — Next time, come to my place.

blocks.text: That last sentence matters: **returning an invitation** is part of Malaysian manners. You don't have to throw a feast — just take them out for a meal, and pay. That closes the circle.

vocab.en: go back to your home village ⚠️
